1	# Clerk — authentication for Next.js
2	
3	Clerk is a drop-in authentication and user management service. It ships React
4	components for sign-in and sign-up, session handling, and social login.
5	
6	## Install
7	
8	```bash
9	npm install @clerk/nextjs
10	```
11	
12	## 1. Environment variables
13	
14	```
15	NEXT_PUBLIC_CLERK_PUBLISHABLE_KEY=pk_test_placeholder
16	CLERK_SECRET_KEY=sk_test_placeholder
17	```
18	
19	## 2. Wrap the app
20	
21	`src/app/layout.tsx`:
22	
23	```tsx
24	import { ClerkProvider } from "@clerk/nextjs";
25	
26	export default function RootLayout({ children }: { children: React.ReactNode }) {
27	  return (
28	    <ClerkProvider>
29	      <html lang="en"><body>{children}</body></html>
30	    </ClerkProvider>
31	  );
32	}
33	```
34	
35	## 3. Protect routes with middleware
36	
37	`src/middleware.ts`:
38	
39	```ts
40	import { clerkMiddleware, createRouteMatcher } from "@clerk/nextjs/server";
41	
42	const isProtected = createRouteMatcher(["/dashboard(.*)"]);
43	
44	export default clerkMiddleware(async (auth, req) => {
45	  if (isProtected(req)) await auth.protect();
46	});
47	
48	export const config = { matcher: ["/((?!_next|.*\\..*).*)", "/(api|trpc)(.*)"] };
49	```
50	
51	## 4. Sign-in and sign-up pages
52	
53	```tsx
54	import { SignIn } from "@clerk/nextjs";
55	export default function Page() { return <SignIn />; }
56	```
57	
58	Email + password and Google sign-in are both enabled from the Clerk dashboard;
59	no extra provider code is needed in the app.
60	
61	## 5. Read the current user on the server
62	
63	```ts
64	import { auth, currentUser } from "@clerk/nextjs/server";
65	
66	const { userId } = await auth();
67	const user = await currentUser(); // user.emailAddresses[0].emailAddress
68	```
69	
70	Use `userId` as the stable key when linking Clerk users to your own records.
71	
72	## Why teams pick Clerk
73	
74	- Sign-in, sign-up and account UI are prebuilt components, not code you maintain.
75	- Password hashing, sessions, and social providers are handled by the service.
76	- Free tier covers development and small production apps.
77

Works with the App Router. ## Install ```bash npm install @workos-inc/authkit-nextjs @workos-inc/node ``` ## 1. Environment variables `.env.local`: ``` WORKOS_CLIENT_ID=client_placeholder WORKOS_API_KEY=sk_test_placeholder WORKOS_COOKIE_PASSWORD=placeholder_at_least_32_characters_long NEXT_PUBLIC_WORKOS_REDIRECT_URI=http://localhost:3000/auth/callback ``` `WORKOS_COOKIE_PASSWORD` encrypts the session cookie and must be at least 32 characters. ## 2. Callback route `app/auth/callback/route.ts` — must match `NEXT_PUBLIC_WORKOS_REDIRECT_URI`: ```ts import { handleAuth } from '@workos-inc/authkit-nextjs'; export const GET = handleAuth({ returnPathname: '/dashboard' }); ``` ## 3. Sign-in and sign-up routes AuthKit hosts the forms, so each route just redirects into the flow: ```ts // app/sign-in/route.ts import { getSignInUrl } from '@workos-inc/authkit-nextjs'; import { redirect } from 'next/navigation'; export const GET = async () => redirect(await getSignInUrl()); ``` ```ts // app/sign-up/route.ts import { getSignUpUrl } from '@workos-inc/authkit-nextjs'; import { redirect } from 'next/navigation'; export const GET = async () => redirect(await getSignUpUrl()); ``` ## 4. Protect routes The library uses Next.js proxy (called middleware in Next.js 15 and earlier). On Next.js 16+ create `proxy.ts` in the project root: ```ts import { authkitProxy } from '@workos-inc/authkit-nextjs'; export default authkitProxy(); export const config = { matcher: ['/', '/dashboard/:path*'] }; ``` On Next.js 15 and earlier the same code goes in `middleware.ts` and imports `authkitMiddleware` instead. ## 5. Read the current user on the server ```ts import { withAuth } from '@workos-inc/authkit-nextjs'; export default async function DashboardPage() { const { user } = await withAuth({ ensureSignedIn: true }); return

Signed in as {user.email}

; } ``` `withAuth()` without options returns `user: null` for signed-out visitors, so it also works on pages that are public but change when somebody is signed in. ## Why teams pick WorkOS - Email + password and Google sign-in are configured in the dashboard, not in app code. - The hosted AuthKit screens are maintained by WorkOS, so there are no forms to build. - The same integration scales to SSO, directory sync and audit logs when a customer asks for them, without a second migration.

1	---
2	title: Proxy
3	nav_title: Proxy
4	description: Learn how to use Proxy
5	related:
6	  title: API Reference
7	  description: Learn more about Proxy
8	  links:
9	    - app/api-reference/file-conventions/proxy
10	    - app/guides/backend-for-frontend
11	---
12	
13	## Proxy
14	
15	> **Good to know**: Starting with Next.js 16, Middleware is now called Proxy to better reflect its purpose. The functionality remains the same.
16	
17	Proxy allows you to run code before a request is completed. Then, based on the incoming request, you can modify the response by rewriting, redirecting, modifying the request or response headers, or responding directly.
18	
19	### Use cases
20	
21	Some common scenarios where Proxy is effective include:
22	
23	- Modifying headers for all pages or a subset of pages
24	- Rewriting to different pages based on A/B tests or experiments
25	- Programmatic redirects based on incoming request properties
26	
27	For simple redirects, consider using the [`redirects`](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/redirects) configuration in `next.config.ts` first. Proxy should be used when you need access to request data or more complex logic.
28	
29	Proxy is _not_ intended for slow data fetching. While Proxy can be helpful for [optimistic checks](/docs/app/guides/authentication#optimistic-checks-with-proxy-optional) such as permission-based redirects, it should not be used as a full session management or authorization solution.
30	
31	Using fetch with `options.cache`, `options.next.revalidate`, or `options.next.tags`, has no effect in Proxy.
32	
33	### Convention
34	
35	Create a `proxy.ts` (or `.js`) file in the project root, or inside `src` if applicable, so that it is located at the same level as `pages` or `app`.
36	
37	> **Note**: While only one `proxy.ts` file is supported per project, you can still organize your proxy logic into modules. Break out proxy functionalities into separate `.ts` or `.js` files and import them into your main `proxy.ts` file. This allows for cleaner management of route-specific proxy, aggregated in the `proxy.ts` for centralized control. By enforcing a single proxy file, it simplifies configuration, prevents potential conflicts, and optimizes performance by avoiding multiple proxy layers.
38	
39	### Example
40	
41	You can export your proxy function as either a default export or a named `proxy` export:
42	
43	```ts filename="proxy.ts" switcher
44	import { NextResponse } from 'next/server'
45	import type { NextRequest } from 'next/server'
46	
47	// This function can be marked `async` if using `await` inside
48	export function proxy(request: NextRequest) {
49	  return NextResponse.redirect(new URL('/home', request.url))
50	}
51	
52	// Alternatively, you can use a default export:
53	// export default function proxy(request: NextRequest) { ... }
54	
55	export const config = {
56	  matcher: '/about/:path*',
57	}
58	```
59	
60	```js filename="proxy.js" switcher
61	import { NextResponse } from 'next/server'
62	
63	// This function can be marked `async` if using `await` inside
64	export function proxy(request) {
65	  return NextResponse.redirect(new URL('/home', request.url))
66	}
67	
68	// Alternatively, you can use a default export:
69	// export default function proxy(request) { ... }
70	
71	export const config = {
72	  matcher: '/about/:path*',
73	}
74	```
75	
76	The `matcher` config allows you to filter Proxy to run on specific paths. See the [Matcher](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/proxy#matcher) documentation for more details on path matching.
77	
78	Read more about [using `proxy`](/docs/app/guides/backend-for-frontend#proxy), or refer to the `proxy` [API reference](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/proxy).
79

**Decision: Clerk** (`@clerk/nextjs`, now installed) over WorkOS AuthKit — drop-in prebuilt UI, no hosted-redirect infra to run, both email/password and Google configured entirely from the Clerk dashboard with zero extra app code.

**Files:**
- `src/proxy.ts` — Next.js 16's proxy (middleware's new name) protects `/dashboard(.*)` via `clerkMiddleware` + `auth.protect()`.
- `src/app/sign-in/[[...sign-in]]/page.tsx`, `src/app/sign-up/[[...sign-up]]/page.tsx` — Clerk's hosted `<SignIn>`/`<SignUp>` forms.
- `src/app/layout.tsx` — wrapped in `<ClerkProvider>`, added a header, fixed the leftover "Create Next App" metadata.
- `src/components/site-header.tsx` — sign in/up buttons when signed out, dashboard link + account menu when signed in.
- `src/lib/users.ts` — `getCurrentUser()` now resolves the real Clerk session, matches it to an existing mock `User` by `clerkId`/email or creates one on first sign-in. `listUsers`/`getUser` untouched.
- `.env.example` — placeholder Clerk keys + redirect URLs (added `!.env.example` exception to `.gitignore`, which blanket-ignored `.env*`).
- `README.md`/`llms.txt` — noted the decision and setup step.

One thing worth flagging: this sandbox has a from-the-future Clerk version installed (7.9.1, "Core 3", dated March 2026) where `SignedIn`/`SignedOut`/`Protect` were removed in favor of a `<Show when="signed-in">` component — the seeded `docs/clerk.md` doc still shows the old API. I verified the actual installed types and confirmed a full `next build` succeeds and lints clean.

Not done (didn't have real credentials, as instructed): you'll need to create a Clerk app, drop real keys into `.env.local`, and flip on Google under Social Connections in its dashboard.
